title: Anatomy of a Good Prompt
description: Learn the simple framework for writing prompts that consistently get excellent results from any AI tool.

data.text: Most people use AI by typing a quick question and hoping for the best. That works — but learning to write good prompts is like learning to ask good questions. It dramatically improves what you get back. The difference between a vague prompt and a structured one can mean the difference between a mediocre paragraph and exactly what you needed.
A strong prompt usually contains four elements. You do not always need all four — but knowing each one helps you diagnose why a prompt failed and what to add next time.

data.caption: The four components of a high-quality prompt — each one narrows the AI's response space toward what you actually want

terms.definition: Background information the AI needs. Who are you? What situation are you in? What has already happened? What constraints exist? Without context, the AI writes for a generic audience and generic situation.

Ask the AI to act as a specific expert persona. This primes it to use the vocabulary, reasoning style, and priorities of that role. "Act as a senior UX designer", "You are a patient high school biology teacher", "Respond as a skeptical investor."
The actual instruction — what you want it to do. Be specific and action-oriented. Use verbs: Write, Summarize, Analyze, Rewrite, Compare, List, Explain. Vague tasks get vague outputs.

How you want the output structured — "give me a numbered list", "write in under 100 words", "use markdown headers", "respond as a table", "write two short paragraphs". Format constraints force precision.

data.text: Before vs. After: three real examples

data.title: Email writing — before
data.content:
Write me an email.

→ Result: A generic email template. Not useful.

data.title: Email writing — after (CRTF applied)
data.content:
Context: I manage a small agency. A client missed our third project check-in without explanation and the deadline is in 4 days.
Role: Act as a professional account manager.
Task: Write a follow-up email that conveys urgency without being confrontational.
Format: Two short paragraphs. Max 80 words. Professional but warm tone.

→ Result: A polished, ready-to-send email that hits all your constraints.

data.title: Content analysis — before
data.content:
Tell me about this article. [paste text]

→ Result: A vague summary. Probably not what you wanted.

data.title: Content analysis — after (CRTF applied)
data.content:
Context: I'm preparing a competitive analysis for our marketing team.
Role: Act as a content strategist.
Task: Identify the three main arguments in this article and evaluate how well each is supported by evidence. Flag any logical gaps.
Format: Numbered list. One sentence per argument, two sentences on evidence quality.

[paste article]

→ Result: A structured, actionable analysis you can use directly in a slide.

data.title: Code review — after
data.content:
Context: I'm a junior developer and wrote this Python function. It works but I'm not confident it's clean.
Role: Act as a senior Python developer doing a code review.
Task: Review this function for readability, edge cases, and any bugs. Suggest improvements.
Format: Use markdown. First show issues as a numbered list, then show the improved code block.

[paste code]

→ Result: A genuine code review with concrete suggestions and revised code.

data.text: You do not have to write the whole CRTF prompt at once. Start with the task, see what you get, then add elements to refine it. Here is what that iteration looks like:

rows: "Explain machine learning"
Too general — could be a textbook chapter or a tweet
"Explain machine learning in plain English, no jargon"
Still too long, no audience
"Explain machine learning to a business executive in 3 sentences, focusing on practical impact"
Much better — but tone could be more direct
"You are a consultant. Explain machine learning value to a skeptical CFO in 3 sentences. No jargon. Start with the business benefit."
✅ Ready to use

data.text: You rarely get a perfect result on the first try — and that's fine. Treat prompting like a conversation: refine, clarify, ask it to adjust the tone, make it shorter, add an example, try again. Follow-up prompts can be simple: "Make it more direct.", "Add one concrete example.", "Cut it to half the length."

items.text: Did I give enough context for the AI to understand my situation?
Did I specify a role or persona if useful?
Is my task instruction clear, specific, and action-oriented?
Did I specify the desired format and length?
Did I include any constraints (what NOT to do, tone, audience)?
If the output was wrong, did I refine rather than restart?

data.title: Takeaways
points: Good prompts have: Context + Role + Task + Format (CRTF)
Specificity is your superpower — vague prompts get vague answers
You do not need all four elements every time — add what's missing when output disappoints
Prompting is iterative — refine the result instead of accepting the first output
The AI cannot read your mind; tell it exactly what you need, for whom, and in what form

data.text: A strong prompt can be diagnosed before execution. Clear role, objective, constraints, and output format reduce ambiguity and lower revision cycles. For practical work, treat prompts as draft specifications that should be iterated with concrete acceptance criteria.

rows: Intent clarity
Is the goal explicit in one sentence?
Add a one-line objective statement
Context completeness
Does the model have enough background?
Provide only the minimum relevant context
Constraint precision
Are boundaries measurable?
Convert vague rules into explicit limits
Output contract
Can quality be reviewed quickly?
Specify format, tone, and evaluation points
